title: American social connection is constrained by time and weak community participation, not simply by individual loneliness
source_unit: Second annual Social Connection in America survey, a RAND and The Connection Institute national tracking initiative with Barnes Family Foundation support; 2026 public findings
geography: United States; national adult social-connection estimates with state-level and future youth-tracking scope

denominator.unit: more than 10,000 U.S. adults administered the annual survey through Ipsos KnowledgePanel; exact public denominator not stated

social_connection_trend.value: key indicators weakened for a second consecutive year

observations.method: Second annual Social Connection in America survey, administered to more than 10,000 people by Ipsos through KnowledgePanel; the initiative is designed for annual trend tracking over 25 years and the 2026 questions were generally maintained with added technology and participation-barrier items.
observations.uncertainty: The public 2026 findings page does not disclose the exact analytic denominator, full weighting details, response rate, or subgroup precision; the cross-sectional annual comparison does not establish why connection changed or whether loneliness caused later outcomes.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults; state-level and youth extensions are part of the initiative’s broader scope.
observations.counterinterpretation: A high loneliness share can coexist with meaningful close relationships, informal support, or temporary stress; weakening indicators do not prove a universal national decline in every dimension of social life.

observations.period: 2026; frequency of contact with loved ones

denominator.unit: more than 10,000 U.S. adults administered the annual survey through Ipsos KnowledgePanel; exact public denominator not stated

infrequent_contact_with_loved_ones.unit: see loved ones no more than once or twice a month

very_infrequent_contact.unit: meet people they care about only a few times a year or less

time_as_top_barrier.unit: percent naming time constraints as a barrier to connection

distance_as_barrier.unit: percent naming distance as a barrier to connection

observations.method: Descriptive estimates from the second annual Social Connection in America survey; the project reports administration to more than 10,000 people through Ipsos KnowledgePanel.
observations.uncertainty: Barrier shares may use a question-specific denominator and are not necessarily mutually exclusive; the summary does not establish whether time scarcity reflects work, caregiving, transport, health, scheduling, or preference.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults reporting social-connection frequency and barriers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Infrequent in-person contact does not equal absent support; distance and time can be offset by calls, visits clustered around events, mutual aid, or other forms of connection not captured by the headline measure.

denominator.unit: more than 10,000 U.S. adults administered the annual survey through Ipsos KnowledgePanel; exact public denominator not stated

virtual_not_equivalent_to_in_person.unit: percent saying virtual interaction satisfies connection as much as in-person interaction

rare_or_never_ai_companion_use.unit: percent reporting they rarely or never use an AI companion

observations.method: Descriptive estimates from the second annual Social Connection in America survey; the project reports administration to more than 10,000 people through Ipsos KnowledgePanel.
observations.uncertainty: The public summary does not define the AI-companion category, frequency thresholds, or question order; these are reported perceptions and behaviors, not evidence that virtual interaction or AI companionship improves or harms wellbeing.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults asked about virtual interaction and AI companionship.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some people may use virtual interaction as a complement rather than substitute for in-person connection; low AI-companion use may reflect low awareness, novelty, access, or question framing.

observations.period: 2026; structured community participation and cross-background interaction

denominator.unit: more than 10,000 U.S. adults administered the annual survey through Ipsos KnowledgePanel; exact public denominator not stated

did_not_volunteer.unit: percent reporting no volunteering in the past year

did_not_attend_religious_services.unit: percent reporting no attendance in the past year

frequent_cross_background_interaction.unit: percent interacting often or all the time with people from different backgrounds or viewpoints

rare_or_never_cross_background_interacti.unit: percent interacting rarely or never with people from different backgrounds or viewpoints

observations.method: Descriptive estimates from the second annual Social Connection in America survey; the project reports administration to more than 10,000 people through Ipsos KnowledgePanel.
observations.uncertainty: Participation categories may overlap and the summary does not provide subgroup denominators, trend standard errors, or causal explanations; nonparticipation in formal institutions does not imply social isolation in informal networks.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults reporting civic, religious, organizational, and cross-background interaction.
observations.counterinterpretation: Formal membership and volunteering can decline while informal neighborhood, family, online, workplace, or mutual-aid relationships remain active; cross-background contact is not automatically trust, equality, or durable cooperation.

related_sources.claim: Official survey page: more than 10,000 respondents administered by Ipsos through KnowledgePanel; 2026 questions generally maintained with added technology and participation-barrier items.
Public release announcing the second annual 2026 findings.

boundary: This record captures public 2026 findings on U.S. social connection, contact frequency, barriers, digital substitution, formal participation, and cross-background interaction. It does not establish causal mechanisms, complete sample or weighting details, individual trajectories, health effects, or whether informal relationships compensate for weak formal participation.
